subtype: Stage 6: Boundaries and a lasting thread [Response]
passage: I'm Ira, and looking back on my year in the robotics club, what I notice most is how ordinary Pema ma'am kept everything. Every message went to the team group, with our parents in it. When I needed help with my code, we sat in the library with the door open, and she mentioned it to Amma at pickup. When I tried to give her a gift after the regional round, she smiled and said a card signed by the whole team was plenty. So in March, when a grown man from an online coding contest messaged me privately, offered me a prize and wrote, "Keep this just between us," something felt wrong at once. I showed Amma that night. She stayed beside me, listened calmly, and said I'd done nothing wrong. Before bed we reported it to the contest organisers and told Pema ma'am.

qa.q: Where did Ira and Pema ma'am sit when Ira needed help with code?
qa.a: They sat in the library with the door open.

qa.q: Why did the stranger's message feel wrong to Ira at once?
qa.a: Ira had learned from Pema ma'am that safe mentors keep things open, so a private offer with "Keep this just between us" felt like a warning sign.

qa.q: What makes Amma's response a wise one?
qa.a: She stayed with Ira, listened calmly, said it wasn't Ira's fault, and acted that same night by reporting it and telling a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Pema ma'am feel on hearing what happened in March?
qa.a: She would likely be concerned but relieved that Ira spoke up, and glad the club's open habits helped Ira spot something unsafe.

grounding: A teen recalls a mentor who kept contact open and shared with parents, and how that helped the teen tell a parent when another adult asked for secrecy.

subtype: Stage 6: Boundaries and a lasting thread [Response]
passage:
Note to the club welfare officer, from Coach Darshan, under-16 football.
Madhav has had a brilliant season and trusts me, which I take seriously. After Tuesday's session he asked for my personal number so we could 'chat anytime', and offered to bring me a jersey from his trip. I thanked him and said no to both, kindly. I explained that all messages go through the team group with parents added, that extra training happens at the ground with others around, and that gifts aren't needed. He looked a bit embarrassed, so I told him he'd done nothing wrong by asking. I also said: if any adult ever asks you for secrets, gifts or private chats, tell your parents or someone you trust. I've copied his mother on this note.

qa.q: What did Madhav offer to bring Coach Darshan?
qa.a: He offered to bring a jersey from his trip.

qa.q: Why might Madhav have looked embarrassed?
qa.a: He may have worried that his friendly request was wrong or that the coach was pushing him away, when he only wanted to stay close.

qa.q: Which steps kept this mentoring safe while keeping it warm?
qa.a: Saying no kindly, keeping messages in the parents' group and training in the open, telling Madhav he did nothing wrong, and informing the welfare officer and his mother.

qa.q: What might Madhav's mother think when she reads this note?
qa.a: She would likely feel reassured that the coach keeps things open and professional, and grateful the safety rule was explained to her son.

grounding: A coach keeps a teen's trust inside open, professional limits with parents and the club informed, and teaches the teen to tell a trusted adult about secrecy or gifts.

passage:
Dear diary, Tuesday night
Coding club was good today. I asked Kunal sir if I could send him my project on a chat app instead of the club group, because I'm shy about people seeing my bugs.
He said no, nicely. He said all his messages go on the club group or by email with my parents copied, so everything stays open. Then he said something I'm writing down so I remember it: "If any adult, even a teacher, asks you to keep secrets, send gifts or talk privately, tell your parents that same day."
At dinner I told Mumma. She said Kunal sir sounds sensible and she's glad to be copied in.
So I posted my buggy code on the group. Two people helped fix it. Not so bad.
Divyansh

qa.q: Where does Kunal sir say all his messages go?
qa.a: On the club group or by email with parents copied.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh want to send the project privately at first?
qa.a: Divyansh felt shy and embarrassed about people seeing the bugs in the code.

qa.q: Which of Kunal sir's choices keeps the mentoring safe, and why?
qa.a: Keeping all contact open with parents copied, and naming secrets, gifts or private talk as signs to tell a parent the same day.

qa.q: How does Mumma see Kunal sir's rule?
qa.a: She sees it as sensible and seems reassured to be included in the messages.

grounding: Shows a mentor keeping contact open and professional with parents aware, and teaching the teen to tell a parent if any adult asks for secrecy.

passage:
Every Sunday the panchayat library in Deepika's village stayed open till noon, and every Sunday Ankita didi sat at the long table with her chemistry books. Other students came and went. Deepika's Amma knew exactly where she was.
This week Deepika brought a small steel box of coconut barfi. "For you, didi. For all the help."
Ankita smiled but pushed it gently back. "Share it with everyone here instead. I don't take gifts from students."
Then she said, more seriously, "If anyone who teaches you ever wants gifts, secrets or to see you alone somewhere, you tell your Amma the same day. Promise?"
"Promise."
Deepika passed the barfi round the table, and the youngest boy took two.

qa.q: What did Deepika bring for Ankita didi?
qa.a: A small steel box of coconut barfi.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she offered the barfi?
qa.a: She felt grateful and wanted to thank Ankita didi for all the help.

qa.q: Which boundary does Ankita didi set, and why does it help keep Deepika safe?
qa.a: She meets only at the open library and refuses gifts, and teaches Deepika to tell her Amma the same day if any teacher asks for gifts, secrets or time alone.

qa.q: How might Deepika's Amma feel about these Sunday lessons?
qa.a: She can feel at ease, because she knows exactly where Deepika is and that others are always around.

grounding: Shows a mentor keeping guidance open and public, refusing a gift and teaching the teen to tell her mother about secrecy or private contact.

subtype: Stage 6: Boundaries and a lasting thread [Response]
passage: Clara had been in Ms Noa Visser's robotics club in Utrecht for three years, and now she was leaving for university. On the last day, Ms Visser gave her a printed list, "People to ask for help at uni", plus her school email. "Write whenever you like. I'll copy your mum in, same as always." Clara laughed. That had always been Ms Visser's way: meetings in the open lab with the door propped, messages through the club group, never private chats. Once, in Year 9, she had told the whole club, "If any adult, including me, ever asks you to keep a secret, gives you special gifts, or messages you privately outside club, tell a parent or another teacher. That's not telling tales. That's staying safe." Clara hugged her goodbye in front of everyone, her dad jingling the car keys, and knew the thread would hold.

qa.q: Where did Ms Visser hold meetings?
qa.a: In the open lab with the door propped.

qa.q: How did Clara feel on the last day with Ms Visser?
qa.a: Clara felt grateful and secure, laughing at the familiar rule and trusting that the thread between them would hold.

qa.q: Which of Ms Visser's habits kept the mentoring safe?
qa.a: Meeting in the open, using the club group instead of private chats, copying Clara's mum on emails, and teaching students to tell a parent if any adult asks for secrecy, gifts or private contact.

qa.q: How might Clara's dad see this mentor?
qa.a: Clara's dad probably feels reassured and trusting, since everything has been open and parents have always been included.

grounding: Shows a mentor keeping the relationship professional and open, and teaching that any adult asking for secrecy, gifts or private contact should be reported to a parent.
